en: The Philippine eagle has a distinctive crest of brown feathers and primarily hunts flying lemurs and monkeys in the rainforests of Mindanao.
The waling-waling orchid is an epiphyte that grows on the branches of tall trees in the Mindanao rainforests to access sunlight.
The tamaraw is a small, hoofed mammal endemic to Mindoro that has V-shaped horns and prefers solitary life in mountainous forests.
The Aedes aegypti mosquito spreads dengue fever in the Philippines by laying eggs in clean, stagnant water inside uncovered containers.
The Philippine tarsier has enormous eyes fixed in its skull, requiring it to rotate its head 180 degrees to spot predators.
The Rafflesia schadenbergiana is a parasitic plant in Mount Kitanglad that lacks leaves but produces massive, foul-smelling flowers to attract pollinating flies.
Philippine coastal ecosystems rely on mangrove trees, which use specialized prop roots to survive in saltwater and block strong typhoon waves.
Every winter, filter-feeding whale sharks migrate to the coastal waters of Donsol, Sorsogon, to feed on abundant plankton near the surface.
The Philippine carabao wallows in mud to regulate its body temperature and protect its sensitive skin from harsh tropical sunlight.
The life cycle of Philippine rice, or palay, begins as a seed, grows into a plant, and produces grain-bearing panicles for harvest.
Filipino children drink calamansi juice because this small citrus fruit is rich in vitamin C, which helps the immune system fight infections.
The Philippine crocodile is a critically endangered freshwater reptile endemic to the country, distinguished by a broader snout and lighter scales.
